title: Thirty-Six Windows on Consciousness: Learning Sanskrit by Taking the Words Apart
claim: Thirty-six short Trika statements from the Śiva Sūtras, Abhinavagupta, Utpaladeva and the Spanda tradition, dismantled until every letter, case ending, compound, verb and sandhi makes sense, so the reader can decide what the ancient authors mean without asking a translation to do the thinking.

purpose.impact: In one sitting the reader watches 'caitanyam ātmā' come apart into two grammatical forms and realizes they can do the same to thirty-five more sentences.
purpose.reader: The Sanskrit-curious reader who wants short authentic statements with reversible proofs, not a full grammar textbook and not a quotation collection.
purpose.realisation: By lesson thirty-six the reader can take an unseen short Trika sentence, reverse sandhi, name cases, and produce a literal translation the grammar warrants.
non_goals: no full critical edition of any of the five works
no invented Sanskrit and no uncollated e-text sold as witness
no promised somatic signs from reading a statement
no padding to a fake page quota

pages.note: Six stages x six short statements; ~2-3pp per reading. Do not pad; final count follows typeset content.

inclusion: every lesson carries the lesson-book anatomy from a witnessed short statement; EXTRACT labelled where cut from a longer verse
word-by-word morphology, reversible sandhi proofs, literal translation before Trika reading, and a transfer exercise per statement
five source works only: Śivasūtra, Śivastotrāvalī, Bodhapañcadaśikā, Paramārthasāra, Spandakārikā — with author attribution kept distinct
devanagari transliterated from IAST at build; IAST copied from editorial/2026-11-08/Trika_Sanskrit_36_Volume_II until print collation
complete parent verse shown beside any EXTRACT so the reader can test whether the excerpt is a whole proposition
overlaps with complete reference books are credited teaching quotation, not a competing claim to own a verse
every lesson carries the ten layers in order, each building on the previous — not independent encyclopedia entries
witness (Devanagari, IAST, author, work, verse, edition) is extract-and-place from translation-work; no invented Sanskrit
morphology, sandhi proofs and syntax are reversible: input → rule → output, with alternatives recorded when commentators differ
translation is demonstrably derived from the grammar before any metaphysics is introduced
Trika exegesis attributes verse, Abhinavagupta, Kṣemarāja, Yogarāja, Lakshmanjoo and our synthesis separately
reading mode keeps irreverent everyday clarity; learning mode never skips morphology or fakes pronunciation
grammar knowledge accumulates: a form mastered in an earlier lesson is reinforced, not re-taught from zero
exclusion: no full Sanskrit edition claimed — this is a teaching selection of 36 statements
no invented Pāṇini numbers and no unverified e-text sold as a critical witness
no sensation-success tests in practice blocks
Spanda authorship stays traditionally attributed; Śivasūtra uses a declared recension (77-slot caution documented in editorial findings)
never invent Sanskrit, etymologies, or Pāṇini rule ids that have not been verified
never silently resolve a parse ambiguity or merge distinct teachers into one voice
never present a modern practice adaptation as an ancient prescription
never print Lakshmanjoo/Dyczkowski prose at length — brief attributed quotation only (house copyright law)
never claim the textbook is the verse's home when a reference volume owns the full text — quotation with attribution only
no PDF build before content, structure and formatting pass — build is last
